summary: Child DNS operators can signal DS or NS changes to the parent with CDS/CDNSKEY (RFC 7344) and CSYNC (RFC 7477) records. This Standards Track document clarifies how these should be kept consistent. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 7477.

eli5.summary: A child leaves notes for the parent about changes to the family address book. This makes sure the notes agree with each other.

questions: what are cds and cdnskey records
why must parents query all nameservers for cds
subtitle: Parents must check that every nameserver of a child agrees before acting on CDS, CDNSKEY or CSYNC records.

tldr.problem: Parent-side entities such as registries and registrars read CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC records from a child zone to update DS and NS records. If they ask only one nameserver, a single faulty or hostile operator can change the whole delegation.
tldr.mechanism: The Parental Agent must query every IP address of every nameserver in the delegation and act only if the responses are plausibly consistent. On an inconsistency it must abort and change nothing.
tldr.outcome: A single operator can no longer unilaterally add or remove trust anchors or nameservers. Delegation changes happen only when the child's operators agree.

today: RFC 9975 is a Standards Track document published in May 2026 and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 7344 and RFC 7477, so its consistency rules apply to CDS/CDNSKEY and CSYNC processing alongside those documents.

sections.title: The Problem with Asking One Nameserver
sections.content:
Changing a DNS delegation means changing the DS and NS record sets on the parent side. RFC 7344 lets a child publish CDS and CDNSKEY records that hold the prospective DS parameters. RFC 7477 defines CSYNC records that signal a desired update of the delegation's NS and glue records. Parent-side entities, such as registries and registrars, can fetch these records and use them to update the delegation.

Section 3.1 of RFC 7477 advises Parental Agents to limit CSYNC queries to a single authoritative nameserver, and Section 6.1 of RFC 7344 says nothing specific about how CDS/CDNSKEY queries should be done. That works in ideal conditions. It breaks when the nameservers are out of sync, for example during a Key Signing Key (KSK) rollover, or when they are run by different entities, as in a multi-signer setup (RFC 8901).

If records come from one nameserver only, each nameserver can trigger a delegation update on its own. One provider in a multi-signer setup could then, accidentally or maliciously, remove another provider's trust anchors or nameservers. A parent also cannot judge the impact of an update unless it inspects all of the child's nameservers, yet an automated update must not break the current delegation (RFC 7344, Section 4.1).
sections.eli5: If the post office believes whoever writes first, one mistaken or sneaky helper can mess up everyone's mail. So it should check with all the helpers.

sections.title: What This Document Changes
sections.content:
This document updates two earlier RFCs and leaves the rest of them alone. Section 4.1 of RFC 7344 lists acceptance rules for CDS/CDNSKEY records, and that list is extended with the consistency requirements defined here.

Sections 3.1 and 4.2 of RFC 7477 contain logic for choosing which nameserver to query for CSYNC information. That logic is replaced by the CSYNC consistency requirements in this document.

The terminology section defines two setups. A multi-provider setup has several providers independently operating authoritative DNS for a domain, usually for redundancy. A multi-signer setup is a multi-provider setup for a DNSSEC-enabled domain with multiple independent signing entities. It may be permanent, for redundancy, or temporary, while changing provider.
sections.eli5: This note edits two older rule books. It swaps out the old advice to ask just one helper and adds a rule to ask them all.

sections.title: Rules That Apply to Every Record Type
sections.content:
The Parental Agent MUST fetch all IP addresses for each nameserver hostname listed in the child's delegation, using a validating resolver and including any available glue. Before acting on any CDS/CDNSKEY or CSYNC record, it MUST have established plausible consistency by querying all of those addresses for the record sets in question.

Consistency is required across received responses only, and a NODATA response counts as a received response. If a nameserver does not answer, the Parental Agent SHOULD try again later before deciding it is permanently unreachable and dropping it. A configurable retry schedule is RECOMMENDED; the RFC gives an exponential back-off of 5, 10, 20, 40, ... minutes as an example, and allows trying from another network vantage point.

If the state is inconsistent, the Parental Agent MUST abort. It MUST NOT delete or alter any existing RRset that would have been changed, and MUST NOT create any RRset that would have been created had the answers agreed. Implementations MAY retry the whole process to cope with transient inconsistencies such as replication delay.

Pending queries can be dropped as soon as a response confirms the status quo, either implicitly (NODATA) or explicitly (a response matching the current delegation), because nothing would need to happen anyway. DNSSEC signatures MUST still be requested and validated for all queries unless otherwise noted.
sections.eli5: Ask every helper, and be patient if one is slow to answer. If they disagree, change nothing. If one already says nothing needs to change, you can stop asking.

sections.title: Consistency for CDS and CDNSKEY
sections.content:
The Parental Agent MUST query all nameservers listed in the child's delegation. Each key referenced in any received answer MUST also be referenced in all other received responses, or the responses must consistently ask for removal of the entire DS RRset (RFC 8078, Section 6).

The state is inconsistent when a key appears in the CDS set but not the CDNSKEY set (or the reverse), or when one nameserver returns a key that another lacks. It is also inconsistent when one response asks to remove the DS RRset while another says no change (NODATA) or gives a DS update.

CDS records are checked for consistency only when their digest type is marked MUST in the "Implement for DNSSEC Delegation" column of the IANA "Digest Algorithms" registry. Records with other digest types can be ignored. The parent may choose its own digest types for the DS RRset as local policy, but the set of keys is not up to policy: the DS RRset is consistent only if it includes all keys from the CDNSKEY RRset and the eligible CDS records.

During initial DS provisioning (DNSSEC bootstrapping), normal validation of CDS/CDNSKEY responses is not yet possible, so authenticated bootstrapping (RFC 9615) should be used.
sections.eli5: Every helper must list the same keys. If one helper has a key the others do not know about, that is a red flag and nothing changes.

sections.title: Consistency for CSYNC
sections.content:
A CSYNC workflow has two steps: query the CSYNC record (and possibly the SOA record) to learn which data to synchronize, then query those data records, for example NS, before placing them in the parent zone. If the conditions below fail, the CSYNC state MUST be treated as inconsistent.

When querying CSYNC, the Parental Agent MUST query all nameservers in the delegation and ensure the record's immediate flag and type bitmap are equal across responses. The SOA serial field and the soaminimum flag may legitimately differ between nameservers, so equality is not required. Instead, each is processed against the SOA record from the same nameserver, and the per-nameserver conclusions about whether the update is allowed must all agree.

When fetching the data record sets named in the CSYNC record (such as NS or A/AAAA), the Parental Agent MUST query all nameservers that returned a CSYNC record and ensure all return equal rdata sets, including the case where all are empty. As a local policy example, a parent may accept glue only for in-domain or sibling NS hostnames.

Other CSYNC processing rules from RFC 7477 stay in place. NS processing happens before glue updates, and address queries go only to in-bailiwick NS hostnames. Parental Agents SHOULD also check that CSYNC-based updates do not break the delegation, for instance by pointing it at nameservers that lack the required DNSKEY records or do not know the zone.
sections.eli5: For the change notes, the helpers must agree on what to change and on the new list itself. They may differ on small bookkeeping details, as long as each one's own details lead to the same decision.

sections.title: Failure Scenarios Without Consistency Checks
sections.content:
Appendix A gives informative examples of what goes wrong when the parent does not enforce consistency.

  • Replication lag: during a key rollover, a lagging nameserver makes the parent see different CDS/CDNSKEY sets, so old and new DS sets alternate and the zone maintainer may break the chain of trust by removing a key still referenced by a stale record.
  • Lame delegation takeover: if a delegation names a nameserver hostname that does not exist, someone who registers it can serve CDS/CDNSKEY records. If the delegation is not DNSSEC-protected and the parent processes those records without a consistency check, the delegation can eventually be secured with the attacker's keys. The attacker can then use CSYNC to remove other nameservers or change glue.
  • Permanent multi-signer: a provider that publishes CDS/CDNSKEY or NS data containing only its own keys or hostnames can cause the other providers to be removed from the delegation.
  • Temporary multi-signer (provider change): if the new provider omits the old provider's keys, the parent's next scan can update the DS set so that it authenticates only the new provider's DNSKEYs, and answers from the old provider fail validation.

The RFC notes that RFC 7344, Section 6.2 already foresaw the replication case, but its solution requires parents to keep state on CDS/CDNSKEY RRsets. This document achieves the same without that burden.
sections.eli5: If the post office listens to only one helper, a helper who made a mistake, or a stranger pretending to be a helper, could cut everyone else out of the address book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The strict rules prevent publication of half-baked DS or NS RRsets that only some of the authoritative nameservers support. They ensure a single operator cannot unilaterally add or remove trust anchors or nameservers when other operators are present, whether the setup is intentional or the result of a lame-delegation hijack. Delegation records change only when zones are synchronized across operators and unanimously reflect the domain owner's intentions, which helps both availability and integrity.

Sometimes consensus cannot be reached, for example when one operator is uncooperative. Parental Agents SHOULD therefore keep accepting DS and NS/glue update requests from the domain owner over an authenticated out-of-band channel such as EPP (RFC 5730), regardless of whether they adopt automated maintenance. The same channel allows recovery if the private key for signing the CDS/CDNSKEY or CSYNC records is lost.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Because everyone has to agree, nobody can sneak a change in alone. If the helpers cannot agree, the owner can still tell the post office directly.

viz.caption: WHAT MUST MATCH ACROSS NAMESERVERS (SUMMARISED FROM THE RFC)

cells: Referenced keys, or a consistent request to remove the whole DS RRset
CDS records with digest types not marked MUST in the registry
Immediate flag, type bitmap, and the NS or A/AAAA data record sets
SOA serial field and soaminimum flag, if each nameserver's own SOA gives the same decision
